title: Israel and Yaakov: the middos of Zeir Anpin, their birth, and the crown of Chabad
overview: Chapter 34 opens the second stretch of the book's account of the middos, the emotional attributes of Zeir Anpin. Its two names are Yaakov and Yisroel. The name Yisroel is the power of MaH, worth forty-five, to refine BaN, worth fifty-two, which stands for the animal soul and nature. Refining needs chachma. Yisroel Saba is the mature middos of chachma, and Yisroel Zuta is the younger middos below it. A drop from the father's brain gives the small Israel its life. The middos are born in stages, from the fetal state through the mochin of yenika, the first maturity of Ima and the second of Abba. A middah is born from the nehi of Abba and Ima; its reason then falls away and it lives on its own. Before nine the intellect serves only the natural middos. From nine a child can want things because they make sense, and from thirteen to twenty the crown of Chabad is revealed, completing the mochin. The chapter ends with the depth of chachma, the chacham who sees potential in others, and the verse that you ruled over Elokim.

sections.title: Two names for the middos of Zeir Anpin: Israel and Yaakov
sections.summary: The chapter opens a new stretch: the middos of Zeir Anpin of Atzilus come in two levels, called Yaakov and Yisroel. This is the frame for the rest of the chapter.

phrases.he: (לד) והנה בבחינת זעיר אנפין דאצילות יש ב' מדריגות
phrases.en: In *Zeir Anpin*, which are the *middos* of *Atzilus*, there are two levels
these are called *Israel* and *Yaakov*, right?
as is known
and so to explain all the details within this

blocks.text: The first large part of the chain of worlds is done: the higher unity, and how everything expresses G-d's will, from the first *tzimtzum* through *Adam Kadmon* down to *Zeir Anpin* of *Atzilus*. The next stretch takes its *middos*: how they go into the *kelim*, how the *orot* relate to them, and how this runs down to *Malchus* of *Atzilus*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 034 recaps the earlier chapters before it reads line 1. Placed before line 1, where the reading starts.

blocks.text: *Zeir Anpin* has different *partzufim*, each one all ten *sefiros* working together in a particular role and focus. *Israel* and *Yaakov* are two of them, two levels of maturity in the *middos*, according to whether the *mochin* are revealed. He will develop them with a *mashal* of growing up.
The *mashal* is how people grow up: the difference between a child and an adult.
blocks.title: A child and an adult

blocks.text: The *nimshal* is G-dliness revealed. When G-dliness is more revealed, with open miracles, that is the more mature state. When it is hidden and looks like nature, it is less mature. The same holds in Torah. The inner purpose of Torah, the central value of G-dliness for a Jew, is the mature side. The outer part, which looks like a system of judgment, is the less mature one.

*Zeir Anpin* of *Atzilus* has two levels, *Israel* and *Yaakov*. *Yaakov* was his first name. He was later given the name *Yisroel* after he overcame an angel. The details of these two levels are the header of this chapter.

phrases.he: הנה תחלה יש להבין בטעם קריאת שם ישראל,
phrases.en: first you have to understand why he was called
because you have ruled, you have fought with an angel and you've come out on top, you've won over an angel

blocks.text: First he goes over the Kabbalah this chapter is based on, then gives analogies, as is his custom. The question is why Yaakov was called Yisroel. The verse says he got the name after he overcame Lavan and the angel of Esau: *ki sarita im Elokim* means that he ruled over an angel and prevailed.

sections.title: Israel as MaH, the name that refines BaN
sections.summary: The line gives the Name MaH, worth forty-five, which rules over and refines BaN, worth fifty-two. Refining takes chachma, and the man's way is to conquer.

phrases.en: and this represents the idea of the name *MaH* that rules over and refines
it says that through the power of *chachma* things are refined
and this relates to the idea that it's the nature of a man to conquer and to change things in that kind of way
is the way of a man to conquer

blocks.text: The Name of G-d is spelled in several ways, when its letters are spelled out (a *milui*). The spelling that adds up to forty-five is *MaH*, which stands for *Zeir Anpin*. The spelling that adds up to fifty-two is *BaN*, which stands for *Malchus*. *MaH* rules over and refines *BaN*. The unity of the two includes all of the *seder hishtalshelus*, all of Torah and *mitzvos*, and all of a person's *avodah*.

These are very general concepts: spirit and body, soul and body, faith and reason. They also stand for the more mature perspective, as in a man and a woman, of a *tzaddik* and the lower perspective of an ordinary person.

sensitivity.reason: Pairs a man and a woman as the two perspectives, a gendered comparison in his own example beyond the line.
sensitivity.publishable: These are very general concepts: spirit and body, soul and body, faith and reason. They also stand for the more mature perspective of a *tzaddik* and the lower perspective of an ordinary person.
sensitivity.judgmentNote: The words 'as in a man and a woman' are an example he gives in passing. A reader may take the pairing as a claim about men and women. Decide whether the public text drops it.

blocks.text: MaH also stands for bitul, humility and transparency to G-dliness, and bitul is what refines BaN, our animal soul, body and nature. In us, the G-dly soul will dominate the body and refine it, changing our habits and our nature. In the world this is G-dliness dominating nature through miracles. In Torah it is the inner G-dliness of Torah, faith coming into the intellect.

Learning and theory guide action, as in the sciences, where a theory is made before an experiment. But once BaN is refined, it gives something to MaH, so the action gives deeper understanding, and the result of an experiment changes the theory. That is why *naaseh* comes before *nishma*. The terms of Kabbalah are general paradigms, which is why he uses this technical language.
blocks.title: Theory and experiment

blocks.text: So Israel is MaH refining BaN. To refine, a person needs *chachma*. Someone without it can only do what he is told and cannot change his nature. A little child is like this. He would eat jelly beans for every meal. Only when he gets the deeper *chachma* does he see that he does not want that, and he changes what he wants, as an adult does.

*Bina* grasps a thing the way it was taught. To apply it to a new situation you need the broader idea behind it, beyond the specifics. A leader needs this vision, to see what is really important, so that he can make the decisions the rules do not settle and adjust the system on that deeper view. That is *chachma*.
blocks.question: Why *chachma* for the refining, and not *bina* or *daas*?

blocks.text: This is true in Torah too. Recognizing the intrinsic value of a Jew, and the intrinsic holiness of G-dliness, is abstract. A decision (*psak*) has to rest on that deeper view, not only on what the books say, or one will face situations where one does not know what to do. *Chachma* settles this: you really get the point, and you could write the book.

A child who does what his mother tells him is fine up to a point. In the world he needs his own sense of right and wrong. That is the idea of a *bar mitzvah*, which we learn from Shimon and Levi. They defended Dina, and though they were teenagers and a little hasty, they did not first ask what was right. They had the strong sense of it on their own. Only when right and wrong come from inside a person is it *chachma*.
The line says that the way of a man is to conquer, to go out and change things.
That is also why the *mitzva* to have children is put on the man, who goes out and initiates, though his wife helps. It is the man's nature to go out to war; women don't really fight wars so much.

sensitivity.reason: Says that it is a man's nature to go to war, and that women do not fight wars. A generalisation about the sexes in his own explanation, not in the line.
sensitivity.publishable: That is also why the *mitzva* to have children is put on the man, who goes out and initiates, though his wife helps.
sensitivity.judgmentNote: The mitzva on the man is a halacha and stays. The war sentence is his generalisation about men and women. A person decides whether it prints.

blocks.text: The male nature to go out and conquer is a metaphor. It stands for the perspective of *chachma*: a person who sees the vision can go out, change things and refine them. He needs that deeper perspective to do it.

sections.title: Israel saba and Israel zuta: the mature and the young middos
sections.summary: Within Zeir Anpin the middos come as Yisroel saba, the grandfather Israel, which is the mature middos of chachma, and Yisroel zuta, the small Israel, which is the lower middos below chachma. A drop from the father's brain gives the small Israel its life.

phrases.en: and the explanation of all of this
first, we have to explain the difference between *Yisroel saba*, which are the *middos* which correspond to *Zeir Anpin*, but the way they are in
the *middos* of *Zeir Anpin* are called the small *Israel* as opposed to *saba*, which means the grandfather *Israel*

blocks.text: *Yisroel saba* are the *middos* of *Zeir Anpin* as they are in *chachma*, the applied *middos* of *chachma* and *bina*, as explained earlier under *tevuna*.

*Yisroel saba* is the intuitive sense of how to apply the intellect: what is right in a given situation, even when you cannot say why. Being able to explain why is *tevuna*, a system for making the decision, the way an engineer might work out the right thing to do.

*Yisroel saba* is the sense of what is holy and right, from being a refined, sensitive person with a good upbringing. That is why sefarim speak of doing things *b'ruach Yisroel saba*, with a holy, proper approach, even just following the spirit of the law. *Yisroel zuta* is the small Israel, as opposed to the grandfather.
The *middos* within *chachma* itself are called the grandfather *Israel*, the sage, the more mature set.
Within *Yisroel saba* there are two levels: the *middos* in *chachma* itself, and those in the *chachma* of *Keser*, called *chachma sesimah*.

The *middos* in *chachma sesimah* are called *Adam Kadmon* in the language of the Zohar. At the start of each chapter the *Mitteler Rebbe* lays out the Zohar's and *Etz Chaim*'s terms, so we can put them together with what is explained here.

The line says, *what is his name, and what is his son's name*: the *MaH* of the *middos* and their *bittul*, which goes from level to level, from the more mature perspective, the father's name, down to his son.

phrases.he: ובחינת המדות שלמטה מן החכמה נקרא ישראל זוטא,
phrases.en: but the *middos* that are lower than *chachma* are called
and those are immature, relatively speaking

blocks.text: The *middos* below *chachma* are *Yisroel zuta*: pure *middos*, not sitting within the *sechel*, and relatively immature.
Here the whole intellect is concealed: the reason for the *middos* is mostly gone, and only the emotions are there.

phrases.he: רק מה שהכלי חיצוניות דנצח והוד דאבא ממשיך להוליד ולהמציא שכל לחסד ואהבה,
phrases.en: But this is just like from the external *Netzach* and *Hod* of *Abba*, that brings out and gives birth to an intellect for *chesed* and love, which is called the small
and then that creates a certain feeling
and this is like the metaphor of how the drop of semen from the father that originates in the father's brain

phrases.he: כו', כך נאמר מה שם בנו שהוא ישראל זוטא, שנמשך לו מטיפת אבא כו' וכידוע)

blocks.text: The small *chesed* comes from the external *Netzach* and *Hod* of *Abba*, which bring out an intellect for *chesed* and love. A person understands something, asks how it applies to him, and a feeling comes out of that. The feeling can stay even when he does not know why he has it, and it can be for good or for bad.

The image is the drop from the father's brain. The child, the small Israel, comes from the father's drop. The child has the essence of the father's ability, but not his knowledge and experience. Those are lost, and the child has to learn from the beginning.
blocks.title: The drop from the father's brain

blocks.text: A scientific account of these metaphors is hard, because the science has changed since the book was written, in the 1700s or early 1800s. The basic idea is that arousal starts in the mind, and a chemical wave floods it, from glands such as the pituitary, probably the main one, which secrete hormones like dopamine and serotonin. Serotonin gives a sense of love and bonding. These hormones trigger the making of the semen, which carries the *koach hayuldah* and the DNA. He thinks the chemicals that make a cell grow very fast relate to the essence of life, which dilutes as the body develops. It is worth researching, he says, but there are many ways to study it.
blocks.title: The brain and the drop

sections.title: Birth of the middos: the lower sefiros of Abba and Ima
sections.summary: The lower three sefiros of Abba, which here stand for chachma, are drawn into the lower sefiros of Ima. The reason for a middah is lowered into a reason, the reason falls away when the middah is born, and the born middah carries the chasadim of Abba and the gevuros of Ima.

phrases.en: So the lower three
they're drawn into

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת השפעת והשפלת השגה וטעם למדת החסד כו'
phrases.en: that then lowers it and brings it down to be a reason for why you should want to do something or why you should love something

blocks.text: The lower three *sefiros*, *netzach*, *hod* and *yesod* of *Abba*, which here stand for *chachma*, are drawn into *netzach*, *hod* and *yesod* of *Ima*. That is the image of procreation: *netzach*, *hod* and *yesod* stand for the reproductive organs.
Here it is the *zivug*, the union from *chachma* to *bina*: a person has an intuitive, essential idea and packages it in an explanation or model, which is *bina*.
This is the lowering of the *hasaga* and the reason for the *middah* of *chesed*: an intrinsic reason, seen in *chachma* and *bina*, brought down to be a reason to want, or love, something.

A parent tells a child, do your homework, because I will give you a candy or a prize. The candy packages the real reason: that learning is true, that it is worth wanting to know it, that one should develop one's potential, and that effort is valuable. A child is immature and cannot yet grasp that intrinsic value, so it has to be packed in a logic that makes sense on his level.
blocks.title: Homework and a candy

blocks.text: The same is true in Torah. The real reasons for the *mitzvos* are the intrinsic value of G-dliness and the nature of our soul, which only a *tzaddik* is mature enough to appreciate. So for a regular person you explain reward, punishment and the blessings he will get: a lower reason, based on the world or the body.

Say you tell a person to put on *tefillin* for the Land of Israel. He should want to do it just because it is what G-d wants, and part of him does. That essence comes across, though it is sometimes packed that way, and that is what works.

There is a great letter of the Rebbe, on chabad.org, that relates to this. He thinks it was written to one of the leaders of Hillel, who asked him questions on campus at the Hillel House, and he forgets exactly the details. The Rebbe says we need different stories to tell ourselves. How you explain to a seventy-year-old why to do something is very different from how you explain it to a five-year-old. Inside each of us there is a seventy-year-old, a five-year-old and a thirteen-year-old, so sometimes the deeper idea has to come down to a lower level to reach a part of us.
blocks.title: Different stories for different parts of us

blocks.text: So the essential idea of *chachma* is packaged, going through the *nehi* of *Abba* into the *nehi* of *Ima*, to be the reason for the *middah*.

phrases.en: but then, so the *nehi* of *Ima* is what we call the *bechin*, just like the reason of why you should do it

phrases.he: בשעת תולדת גלוי התפעלות מדת האהבה
phrases.en: But then when the actual *middah* is born, that reason kind of goes away, and you just feel the feeling

phrases.he: כנראה בחוש שמתקצר ומסתלק הטעם והשכל בשעת התפעלות המדה
phrases.en: like we see that when the person actually gets the feeling and gets excited, the reason goes away and they just feel the experience of the happiness
and this is the deeper, one of the deeper meanings of what Pharaoh told the midwives when he wanted them to kill the Jewish children as soon as they were born
he gave them a sign how they should know that they were about to give birth. It says, when you see them on the birthing stone
that the legs become cold like stone at the time of childbirth

phrases.he: שנסתלקו נה''י הראשונים ונמשכים נה''י חדשים כו'
phrases.en: as soon as you see that their legs get cold, you know they're about to give birth
that when the original *nehi* has to leave, and then a new *nehi* comes

blocks.text: The *nehi* of *Ima* is the *bechin*, the reason: why you should do it. When the *middah* is actually born, that reason goes away, and you just feel the feeling.

Take a child you want to work hard on his homework. At first you tell him to do it for the prize, a reason made by *bina* from the *nehi* of *Ima*. Once he succeeds, he feels the joy, the reason falls away, and he is left with the feeling, which has the essence of *chachma*. Extrinsic motivation is fine when it leads to that feeling. Craft it carefully: it is a hook to bring the child to the intrinsic motivation, not the whole reason.
blocks.title: The prize and the feeling

blocks.text: You can see this by the senses: when a person gets excited by a feeling, the reason goes away. He feels the happiness, fear or anger, and is not thinking about why. It is something deeper than the reason.

This is the deeper meaning of Pharaoh's words to the midwives, when he wanted them to kill the Jewish children at birth. He gave them a sign: when you see them *al ha'avanim*, on the birthing stones. The Sages say the legs grow cold like stone at childbirth, so when the legs get cold, birth is near.

The metaphor: to give birth, the original *nehi* has to leave and new *nehi* come; the feeling in the legs goes cold, and afterwards new *nehi* come out. Similarly, an act done for one reason later gets a new reason once the first goes away. This is explained elsewhere.

phrases.he: ונקרא בחינת בקיעת יסוד דאימא להוליד המדה
phrases.en: And this is called the like the breaking of the water or the splitting

phrases.he: ותחלה כלולה האהבה בהעלם מכוסה בשכל, כעובר במעי אמו כו'
phrases.en: But originally, that feeling of love or whatever any other feeling was originally hidden within the intellect like a fetus inside the mother's womb

phrases.he: אבל לאחר שנולדו המדות הרי הם כלולים מחסדים דאבא וגבורות דאימא
phrases.en: Once they're born, they have this combination of both
together with the more limited packaging

blocks.text: The breaking of the water is the splitting of the *yesod* of *Ima* to give birth to the *middah*, which then becomes independent beyond the reason.

At first the love is hidden in the intellect, like a fetus in the mother's womb. The mind builds a framework for why one should want this and how it fits who one is. An immature person's feeling has to take that form before it can be born. Once experienced, it holds something deeper than what the mind understood, and it grows up, like the father.

Once born, the *middos* include the *chasadim* of *Abba* and the *gevuros* of *Ima*, in general and in each particular *middah*: the living sense of an intrinsic appreciation from *chachma*, with the limited packaging from *bina*.

sections.title: Three stages of mochin: nursing, the mother, the father
sections.summary: The middos pass through three stages: the mochin of yenika (nursing), the first maturity of Ima and the second maturity of Abba. The middos begin in the fetal state, in the external actions, and gain intellect in stages through childhood.

phrases.en: so specifically there are three levels
There is what's called the intellect of

phrases.he: ובחינת מוחין דגדלות ראשון דאימא וגדלות שני דאבא כו' כידוע.
phrases.en: Then there's the first level of maturity, which is called the maturity

blocks.text: Once born, the *middos* go through stages of development, from less mature to more mature. There are three levels of *mochin*: *yenika*, the first maturity of *Ima*, and the second maturity of *Abba*.

*Yenika* is the intellect of suckling: the child is first nursed and cared for, even when a little older. Then come the first maturity of *Ima* and the second of *Abba*. The simple picture: a child first nursed by the mother, then raised by her, and when older, raised by the father.
blocks.title: Nursing, then the mother, then the father

blocks.text: The *Shulchan Aruch* speaks of this idea. Until about six, or five by our count, a child is with his mother. When he reaches school age the father is to start teaching him or send him to school. That is the second maturity.

phrases.en: so to explain this
it's known
So the *middos* start out in a state that's called *ibur*, which is like a fetus, the fetal position, the head is between the knees
just the external aspect, that's what you see

phrases.he: ובהם כלול בהעלם חב''ד וחג''ת כו'
phrases.en: Inside that *nehi* is included the intellect and the emotions, all that's going to come out later

phrases.he: והוא רק בחינת טבעיות המדות כו'
phrases.en: and so that initial *nehi* is what's just the natural

phrases.he: וביניקה מתגדלים להיות בהכנה לקבל מוחין,
phrases.en: and then through as they are being nursed

phrases.he: והוא כמו התינוק שמתגדלים אבריו מיניקת חלב אמו
phrases.en: like a child that the baby first just has to be nursed from the mother's milk
physically and spiritually, the child just has to be nursed and nourished

blocks.text: The *middos* start out in *ibur*, like a fetus with its head between its knees. A fetus's brain is hardly used: it is fed straight into the stomach through the umbilical cord, so everything goes directly into the *nehi*. After birth it gets its own brain and feeds through its own *chachma*. So the *middos* start with *chabad* inside *chagat*, *chagat* inside *nehi*, all packed up in the external actions.

Education begins with doing. You tell the child: stand here, do this, hold this. He does not understand it, feels nothing about it, and is not motivated yet. With no experience, context or knowledge to be interested, you start with just the doing.
The Rebbe advised a man going to yeshiva for the first time, after university, not to ask what he is doing there for six months, since he lacks the context to answer.
blocks.title: The Rebbe's advice to a new yeshiva student

blocks.text: It starts with the *nehi*, which includes the intellect and emotions to come out later. You first need enough experience before you can make sense of it and decide how you feel. So you teach anybody by saying stand here, do this, hold this, and giving the experience. Then you explain what they did and why it works; then they understand, and feel the emotion of having done it right or wrong.

The film *Karate Kid* is an over-the-top version of this. A master has the boy do one thing after another, paint the fence, wax on, wax off, over and over, and only later does the boy see why, and it helps him tremendously. It is unrealistic, a Hollywood montage of forty years of experience in thirty seconds. But the essence is right: first you have the discipline to just do it, and from there you gain the understanding and the mastery.

This is *naaseh* before *nishma*: you have to do before you understand, and to experience something you must be ready to commit to it without understanding. Second-guessing is not doing it. Sometimes it takes a leap to jump in.

That first *nehi* is only the natural *middos*. They are not self-directed. A baby has instincts: it wants to eat and sleep, and when something is uncomfortable it cries. The parent nurtures it according to that nature. The same with anyone: when they first start learning something new, you help nurture the primal things they have inside them.

Through being nursed and looked after, the child grows physically, until he is ready intellectually to be taught intellectual things. By two, three or four a child can start to understand, and you can start teaching him.

The body has to grow strong before the brain can spare the energy to think. A baby cannot even hold up its head, which is big and heavy. The brain has to learn the basics of the world by seeing, hearing, tasting and touching. He notes an analogy with artificial intelligence: to train a model, you first feed in a great deal of data and let the system sort it, before you can direct or teach it.
blocks.title: Training an AI model

blocks.text: Physically and spiritually, the child has to be nursed and nourished first.

phrases.en: until when the child gets to be six years old
so now their emotions have a little bit of intellect

phrases.he: אך בבחינת הטעם ושכל לנהוג בכל דרכיו,
phrases.en: but it's only enough of an intellect and enough of understanding just to like do things

blocks.text: Until about six, which by our count of years may be five, a child is at school age and his emotions have a little intellect. He can understand a little of what is right and wrong, and his likes and dislikes are not only what was pre-programmed into him. A baby is born wanting to nurse, and is naturally afraid of certain things. But by a certain age a child develops preferences from experience and understanding: a child raised around animals may like them, and one who was not may fear a dog.

You can teach a child some control of his impulses, for example potty training: he cannot make on the floor, he eats with a fork and knife and not by smearing food. Around that age a child is expected to have basic control of himself, follow basic manners, and play with others to a degree. That is the idea of *mochin* in contraction.
At this age a child has just enough intellect to act with understanding, and to act like a person and not like an animal: basic cleanliness and basic manners.

In the *Frierdiker Rebbe*'s writings about education, the first thing in *chinuch* is the simple difference between an animal and a person: to be clean, to be neat, to have basic manners, to say please and thank you. People like to go straight to Torah and *mitzvos*, and those are important, but *derech eretz kadma l'Torah*: basic manners come before Torah. That is the real foundation at that age.
blocks.title: The Frierdiker Rebbe on education

blocks.text: Whatever a person did not learn as a child, he learns as an adult. We keep learning as we age, either because we were not taught as children or because there are subtler things to appreciate. People do not always appreciate the importance of these basic things. There is truth to the saying that cleanliness is next to G-dliness.

Training a child to like being clean and neat, to say please and thank you, is really important. It teaches a little impulse control: not just to grab something or demand food, but to ask. It trains him to acknowledge the other person, not to see people only as a means to get what he wants, but to have empathy and take them into account. These little things plant the seeds of the maturity that will come later.

A little child needs constant reminders. He can understand what he is told and can do it, but he does not want to on his own, and does not appreciate why. So you can train him in habits and procedures, like washing hands, brushing teeth, and eating healthy food and not candy. It is a very little self-control, but it is something.

sections.title: Age nine: the intellect starts to shape the middos, and the animal soul
sections.summary: Halacha marks stages of chinuch: zero to three, three to six, six to nine, and nine. From nine a child can want things because they make sense. Before nine the intellect only serves the middos he already has, like an animal's cunning. The section ends with a long turn on fantasy, marketing and the media, and what matures a person.

phrases.en: that then they're, it's kind of like the youngest age that a boy could have a child

phrases.he: שאז הוא בחינת גדלות המוחין יותר,

blocks.text: Halachically, the first stage of *chinuch* runs from zero to six, and more exactly from zero to three and from three to six. Zero to three is mainly the care of physical needs. At three a boy gets his first haircut, the *upsherin*, and girls start lighting candles, which gives them a sense of identity as a Jewish boy or girl. From three to six we train them in basic things, how to dress and to be clean. At six, *chinuch* starts in many matters, because a child can understand to do things.

*Chinuch* in many matters continues until nine, the next halachic milestone. Halachically, at nine we consider a boy to be beginning puberty, and if he has intimacy at that age, we consider it to be legally significant.

sensitivity.reason: States a halachic position on intimacy at nine as legally significant, in loose terms a reader could take as a ruling about children.
sensitivity.publishable: *Chinuch* in many matters continues until nine, the next halachic milestone. Halachically, at nine we consider a boy to be beginning puberty.
sensitivity.judgmentNote: The halacha stays, the sentence about intimacy is dropped in the public text. A person should check the halachic wording against the source before it is printed.

blocks.text: From nine a child is ready to have children: that is the youngest age for a boy, and maybe for a girl, about when puberty starts. There are extreme cases younger, but that is the general halachic idea.

A person begins to be able to reproduce, physically, emotionally, psychologically and spiritually, only once he has enough strength for himself. By nine a child has *nehi* (zero to three), *chagat* (three to six) and *chabad* (six to nine), the full set of *sefiros*. What develops now is something extra, the ability to relate to other people, which is the idea of reproduction.

At nine the intellect becomes a greater maturity, beyond what the *middos* alone need. Until nine the intellect only understands what it is told, and knows what to do. From nine, a child can learn in a pure and abstract way, for its own sake, and appreciate things that have intrinsic value.

blocks.text: From nine, the *middos* can begin to be formed by the intellect alone. A child of nine can want something just because it makes sense to him. Until then he wants what he naturally wants, and may hold off a little with some self-control to get a lollipop. From nine he starts wanting things because he understands that they are good.

This stage runs from nine to bar or bat mitzvah. The intellect is greater than the *middos* need, so it can produce a new *middah*. If the intellect tells the child to want the opposite, he will want the opposite. Eventually all his *middos* are based only on the intellect: what he likes and fears depends on what he understands to be good, bad, right and wrong.

Before nine a child has no *mochin*. He has only the *middah* that is already imprinted in him, and his intellect serves only to work out how to get what he already wants. An animal has a nature put into it, and it can be very clever at solving a maze for food, but it never works out that it should want something outside its nature and change that nature.

The unique human ability to think about oneself and have a self-image starts only at nine, and develops until bar or bat mitzvah, when a person is considered a mature adult, at least in this first stage.

There is a second maturity from thirteen to twenty. The milestones are three, when the boy's *upsherin* and the girls' candles begin; six, when children go to school; nine, another big stage; and bar or bat mitzvah, the next big stage. Twenty is the completion. The main thing is the ability to have a sense of right and wrong on one's own, not just to do what one is told.

Animals too are cunning in how they find their food. In a person this level is called the animal of a person, the animal soul. Its emotions are born with us because of bodily needs, and its intellect only goes to work out how to get what we want. It is not telling us what we should want. That is enough to understand.

The progression from zero to nine is a progression of *katnus*. Until nine a person has only his natural, inborn *middos*; even as he gets smarter, he gets smarter at being who he already is, and does not change his priorities.

They say the difference between men and boys is the price of their toys. An adult can still be a child: as a kid he wanted a little toy truck, and now a big, real one. If his priority is just toys, he is following his animal nature, and is still a child.
A lot of the role models, and the influencers on social media, are, he says, just adult children. There is no sense of meaning or purpose there.

sensitivity.reason: Calls influencers and role models 'adult children', a contemptuous label for a group of people, in the public text.
sensitivity.publishable: A lot of the role models, and the influencers on social media, are, he says, just immature people. There is no sense of meaning or purpose there.

blocks.text: Media create fictional characters, or take movie stars and rock stars and build a persona around them, that look like a happy life people should want. They are the characters who do whatever they want and always get the girl and outsmart everyone, like James Bond. But that is a fantasy. Living that way does not work, is not right, and is not meaningful or happy. You cannot run around dodging bullets and always stay one step ahead.
blocks.title: Fantasy heroes

blocks.text: They offer the fantasy like a promise of candy to a child. It is a way of selling, the same as a stranger who comes to a child and says, you want some candy? The marketing industry does this as well: it tries to trigger natural, animal desires in order to manipulate people.
blocks.title: The creepy stranger and the candy

blocks.text: Marketing uses models who are unrealistically beautiful. They are made to starve themselves and spend their time in the gym to look that way, and then they use Photoshop to make them look even better. The aim is to trigger the natural *middos* and override people's reason, so that they buy things. It is manipulation.
Today there are AI-generated models with fake accounts on social media, and people follow them. They are not real.

The animal soul is very prone to be influenced by fantasies and imagination, because it has no real intellect. Real intellect is like a light that shines through darkness and sees through fantasies; the intellect of the animal soul does not know what is true and right. Shown an image, it readily believes it, and wants or fears what it shows.

Fear-mongering in the media is total poison. It is the emotional and psychological equivalent of eating donuts or candy all the time: it feeds fantasies that make people want things or fear things, just because it sells. He highly recommends staying away from all of that.

Learning a *farbrengen* of the Rebbe, by contrast, is wholesome and empowering. It has real leadership, real meaning, a real vision, and something of real intrinsic value. It is inspiring because it looks into you, finds the inner potential and helps you bring it out. A real mentor who sees your potential and pushes you is hard work, but you know you are moving toward something real and growing.

Much of today's media leaves people in an infantile state, or drives them back to it. Shlomo HaMelech said that all of this is *tavirei d'ruach*, vexing to the spirit. Worldly pursuits and worldly views only create stress, and that is not good.
Once a person matures and has a deeper perspective, his priorities differ: he is not interested in the lure, and sees through it. That is the level of *katnus* in the *mashal*.

sections.title: From nine: the maturity of Abba, the intellect over the middos
sections.summary: From nine a child begins the second maturity of Abba, in which the intellect can overpower the middos. Puberty is the sign that a person can bring something new into the world, and that depends on having the essence of the middah, not only its revealed parts.

blocks.text: From nine the child is ready for the second maturity of *Abba*, the first being *Ima*'s, which lets him follow his mother's instructions. From nine to thirteen the second develops: a sense of what is meaningful beyond the body, the *g-dly soul* and the *yetzer tov*, willing to give up what he wants.

Shimon and Levi risked themselves to save their sister Dina from what they felt was a great injustice. This is *mesiras nefesh*. Naturally a person does not want to risk his life, but a deeper sense can show him that something is more important than himself and what he wants.
blocks.title: Shimon and Levi and Dina

blocks.text: That is the basic idea of becoming a *bar mitzvah* or *bat mitzvah*: at that age a person is old enough to see that something matters more than what he wants, and to be ready to sacrifice for what is right. From nine, this second maturity of *Abba* begins.

Here the intellect should overpower the *middos*, *moach shalit al halev*: what a person understands should change how he feels. This is explained at length elsewhere, from *meirosh tzurim* (the head of the peaks), where he says he saw them.

That is why a person can start having children at this age. Puberty is a big physical change that also starts a change in the mind. A child's job is to be self-centered and to get what he needs to grow. Once he reaches puberty, his brain starts rewiring: he is no longer only here for himself. He is here to be part of a family, to create one, to take care of other people and to be part of a society. Halachically, to count as an adult a person needs both the age and the physical signs of puberty, because those changes have to happen for him to be a *kli* for this maturity.
That is why they can start reproducing: then each of their *middos* already has all nine *sefiros*, *chabad*, *chagat* and *nehi*.

phrases.en: because the intellect was very limited, just according to the natural middos of what they naturally wanted

blocks.text: When the *mochin* of each *middah* have grown in *chabad*, then the *nehi* have the power to give birth, because the two depend on each other. You can only do what you are told until you really get it. Once you get the spirit of the law, you can start making new decisions on your own.

That is the idea of giving birth to something: *the children of tzaddikim are their good deeds*, so you can start doing good deeds based on your own sense of right and wrong. Physically, you have children and learn to care for someone else, giving up sleep and comfort to change diapers in the middle of the night, because something bigger than what is comfortable for you matters.

Being able to create something new, and to relate to someone much lower than you, both depend on seeing that your essence is bigger than your accomplishments. A child has only your essence and no revealed qualities. The ability to relate to such a child is the idea of *chachma*: you see that all people, from the biggest to the smallest, go through the same process of growing and learning, and that external differences are not the point.
So too in Torah: physical *mitzvos* are holy, and one should appreciate the holiness in them, not only in things that are overtly holy, and not only in sitting and learning all day.

The Alter Rebbe and the Baal Shem Tov say, *I don't want your olam haba, I don't want your gan eden, I just want You*. When a person appreciates the essence, once he has the essence he can bring it down and relate to the simplest, lowest person, because it is not about the revelations but about the essence.

A person needs enough maturity to get the essence before he can create something new or influence someone else. A teacher, a *shliach*, or anyone who wants to inspire another has to find that essence in himself. Teaching information is not enough: you have to see the inner potential in the other person and turn it on.

As he explained at length in chapter 26, it takes more wisdom to give simple *mashalim* to a little child than to understand the thing yourself. Bringing it down so simply shows you have its essence; the two depend on each other.
At six, each *middah* has only *chagat* and *nehi*. The *mochin* are very limited, and the *middos* work only according to the natural tendencies of what the child wants.

sections.title: Thirteen to twenty: the crown of Chabad and the completion of the mochin
sections.summary: From thirteen to twenty a person reveals the crown of Chabad, the essence in each middah. He can change his will from above the intellect and can sell his father's estate, which in the mashal means changing what he wants. Halacha gives the age limits, and the Kabbalah explains the ages by the sefiros.

phrases.he: וגדלות שני, היינו מבן י''ג עד ך',
phrases.en: and then the second type of maturity, is from 13 to 20
and that's why, halachically, even though we say 13, a person's a full adult, they're not quite a full adult in Torah when they're 13
they're an adult for some things, but if they inherit property, they're not allowed to sell their estate until they're 20

blocks.text: The second maturity runs from thirteen to twenty. In the sources of Kabbalah, bina and chachma each have two stages. In bina, the first runs until six and the second from six to nine. From nine, the immature side of chachma develops until thirteen, or twelve for girls: a person recognizes that something has intrinsic value and does it with *mesiras nefesh*, giving up what he wants. From thirteen to twenty he gains the ability to change his nature, so that he wants to do it and enjoys it. That is full adulthood, the complete second maturity of *Abba*, at twenty. He notes that the text as written puts this at nine to thirteen, and that it would be worth checking the manuscripts for another version.

Halachically a person is an adult at thirteen, but not quite a full adult in Torah. He is an adult for some things, yet if he inherits his father's estate he may not sell it until twenty, because thirteen-year-olds do not appreciate the value of property. They just want money to go out and party.

sensitivity.reason: A jab at thirteen-year-olds as a group: they want money only to go out and party. Contempt beyond the halacha's reason.
sensitivity.publishable: Halachically a person is an adult at thirteen, but not quite a full adult in Torah. He is an adult for some things, yet if he inherits his father's estate he may not sell it until twenty, because thirteen-year-olds do not appreciate the value of property.

blocks.text: Likewise we do not let people go to war until twenty, because they do not have the maturity for situations where all of one's emotions are thrown out of whack and temptations wear one down.

The metaphor of the father's estate: the person cannot yet change what he wants, because he lacks full mastery of *chachma*, the father's estate. Whether the age should be twenty is complicated, he says, and he does not know. Eighteen-year-old soldiers may not drink until twenty-one, and people complain. Sometimes people do things out there that they should not, being too immature for the situation. Maybe they should be trained younger and not see combat until twenty, but he does not know.

In other words, then the person is able to really recognize the

blocks.text: Now they have the *keser chabad*, the essence of each *middah*, and can change their *ratzon* and *taanug* within every *middah*, changing it from something higher than its own intellect. They recognize something beyond intellect and appreciate it. At twenty comes the complete maturity of the *mochin* of the *middos*.

Then they can sell the inherited estate: with the *mochin* of *Abba*, the root and source of the *middos*, they change things from one *reshus* to another. They recognize the *mochin* of *Abba*: the inner idea at the core, beyond the intellect itself, and appreciate the *emunah* as it is brought into the inner. It is not based only on logic; logic is there to express that higher source and bring it out.
A leader's job is often to make, codify and interpret laws, based on understanding the real inner point. That is real leadership, and real maturity is having that perspective.

Changing from one *reshus* to another means moving from the *nefesh habehamis* to the *nefesh haelokis*, from the mundane to the G-dly. That is where a person can really be a *mashpia*: go out, change things, and make them G-dly.

Until he has that maturity, a person is trying to gain self-control and mastery of himself. Once he has it, he asks how to influence the world: the idea of conquering the world, of going out to war. He must first have that maturity in himself.

Kabbalah sets the ages in these terms: zero to three is *nehi*, three to six *chagat*, six to nine *chabad*, all within the *middos*. From nine to thirteen the *keser chabad* begins to be revealed, in four stages like the four compartments of the *tefillin*, which stand for appreciating what is higher than one understands and committing to it. That is becoming a man.
From thirteen to twenty, seven years, revealing the seven *middos* of *Atik*: being able to have a *taanug*, an enjoyment, in what is right.

Girls have their bat mitzvah at twelve, because they already have the *keser* revealed from the start: they need no special *avodah* to reveal it, because of the nature of women. That is how Kabbalah explains it, for the numbers. This is changing from one *reshus* to another.

sensitivity.reason: Gives the nature of women as the reason girls have the crown revealed from the start. A generalisation about women in his own explanation of the numbers, beyond the source.
sensitivity.publishable: Girls have their bat mitzvah at twelve, because they already have the *keser* revealed from the start: they need no special *avodah* to reveal it. That is how Kabbalah explains it, for the numbers. This is changing from one *reshus* to another.
sensitivity.judgmentNote: The Kabbalistic reckoning of the ages is his own gloss here. The words 'because of the nature of women' are his explanation, not the source. A person decides whether the public text keeps the Kabbalah without them.

sections.title: Depth, Israel, and the leader who refines: the closing of the chapter
sections.summary: The depth of chachma lets a person explain in new ways, not only repeat what he was taught. Israel, the crown of Chabad, makes a person's conviction his own, able to refine BaN. The chapter ends with the verse that you ruled over Elokim, and with a leader who sees the potential in others.

phrases.he: כמו על דרך משל שינויי צירופי האותיות של השכל,
phrases.en: And this is like the ability to take something and explain it in totally new ways

phrases.he: שבא מצד שרש ומקור של עומק השכל ממקורו העצמי דוקא
phrases.en: that requires that you have the real essence of the idea

phrases.en: there's the difference between plagiarism where you're just copying the same words

blocks.text: This is being able to take an idea and explain it in totally new ways, not just repeating what you were taught. You could write the book. That requires the real essence of the idea, which comes only when a person gets the *keser*, the *omek*, the depth: back to the *omek*, *orech* and *rochav* of the first chapter.
Once a person has the *omek*, he can bring the idea all the way down into *mashalim*.

Copying the same words is plagiarism. Using an idea in one's own words is legal. Deeper still, a person has his own idea, which he sees and experiences directly. What he learned may have helped him reach it, but it is his understanding, not egotistical, and he knows it because he sees it, not because someone told him.
Maturity is seeing what is right and wrong not because it says so somewhere, but because you see it and feel it. As we explained in chapter 26, this is a *chacham muflag*, who has the *keser*.

With *omek* a person can bring things down into very simple *mashalim* for a little child. Take the *Moreh Nevuchim*, the Guide for the Perplexed: it speaks very philosophically, which does not reach most people. A true leader packages the essence so that a five-year-old can understand it. That is the idea of our latkes on Chanukah, because of the oil: very simple, yet it gives over the essence.
blocks.title: The Guide for the Perplexed and the latkes

But once they have this deeper maturity of the *keser*, that's called

blocks.text: When a person has this deeper perspective, the *keser chabad*, that is called *Israel*. Until then, the *middos*, while they are immature, are called *Yaakov*.

With this deeper maturity of the *keser*, it is called *Israel*, *lamed rosh*: I have a head, my own mind and perspective. I see it, and am not just doing what I am told. *Umochin*: my own intellect, appreciating that something has intrinsic value. Simply, this is what happens once a person is mature, around twenty, with the *keser chabad*.

The *Rambam* says this in his introduction to *Perek Chelek*, about the thirteen fundamental beliefs of Judaism: when a person comes to understand them, they unlock the *g-dly soul*. The sign is that he wants to know the truth because it is true, and does what is right because it is right.

Such a person has intrinsic motivation: he does not act for reward and punishment, anything outside him, or only because the Torah says so. He recognizes the G-dliness in himself and in the world, connects to it and brings it out. That is the idea of *Israel*.

This is the ultimate maturity of the *mochin*, and so a person can refine *BaN*. Put simply, it is the difference between a *beinoni* and a *tzaddik*. A *beinoni* does what he is told but does not understand it for himself. A *tzaddik* understands it himself. Every person can have this in some ways and not in others.

With this deeper maturity a person can be a *mashpia*, changing his own nature and the world around him. But he has to really get it: doing what you are told can have some effect, but you cannot really make a *dira b'tachtonim*, a G-dly thing below, without being turned on in this deeper way.

There are two levels of *birur*. The first is self-control, *itkafia*, learning to control yourself and to delay gratification. That is the first maturity, of *Ima*. The second is to see that there is something more important than what I want. Then I want to bring that out, to be a creator and a contributor, and to bring goodness, truth and wisdom into the world. The things I wanted as a child now serve as *kelim*, means to accomplish this.

So I see all of those things as *kelim* for *Elokus*, but I value the *Elokus*. Simply: I want to be a creative contributor, knowing the truth and spreading it, and that is the idea of reproduction. A *Rebbe* or a *tzaddik* who brings that perspective to other people has spiritual children. With the perspective of *pnimius haTorah* a person shifts from learning as a *mekabel*, learning to be shown what to do, which is the first necessary stage of self-discipline, to being a *mashpia*, who has it and is ready to bring it out to others.

blocks.text: This is the name *Elokim*, the nature of the world and of ourselves. A person who gets the depth of things can master the world physically, in technology and science, creating a spaceship, which used to be impossible. That is the simple meaning; here the point is deeper.

To refine one's own nature, or the world's, and be its master, one needs this perspective, from the *koach mah* of the *keser* of *chachma* coming into the *middos*. When a person lets these inner truths guide him, he can really be a master.

A very wise person, who knows an idea's depth from its first source, knows how to refine, clarify and remove mistakes. A less wise person who finds a printing error will not notice it: 'that is what it says, I just know how to read.' Someone who really gets it says, no, that must be a mistake, and corrects it.
blocks.title: The printing error

so then they have this deep in sense of like, I look inside myself

phrases.en: and now I'm contributing something to the world, I'm being a creator

blocks.text: His wisdom can also earn him a living, in a trade or business: *Torasho umanuso*, his Torah is his trade. Simply, he is a professional scholar; here it means Torah becomes practical. A person sees how it applies to the physical world, and it can help him succeed physically, because it is not stuck in the intellect.
The real visionaries did not do surveys to see what people wanted. Steve Jobs, for example, had a vision of what would be good, developed it, and then convinced people that this was what they wanted.
blocks.title: Not a survey

blocks.text: The simple meaning is that his business is Torah. When you have the essence, you can bring it down into something practical.

This is the idea that a man's way is to conquer. When a person has this deeper *MaH* of *chachma*, he sees the gifts that G-d gave him and that he can contribute to the world, and so he becomes a creator. Today too there are creators, a creator economy, where people support those who love making and creating things, because those people feel they have something to contribute. You cannot succeed by copying somebody's system. That is a fantasy.
You need something of value to contribute to the world, and to believe in it. That vision has to guide you; that is where a visionary and leader can be successful.

It is the same spiritually. Torah and *mitzvos* come from seeing the spiritual potential of the Jewish soul and of a G-dly world. The *Baal Shem Tov* saw that potential, as the ground has infinite potential, and wanted to bring it out. That is the idea of a Jewish leader, like a real parent.

A parent sees that the child does not yet appreciate why he should learn, but sees the potential in him and works to bring it out. A person with this perspective sees that potential in himself, in others and in the world, and tries to unlock it.

A person with this is a successful mentor. He is not moved by hardship; his whole system of priorities and judgment comes from a deeper place. He has heard many times that the Rebbe took time over a matter, but once he decided he never changed his mind. If it is right, nothing stops him: he is master of the world, and the world is not master of him.

It may be hard, so there must be deliberation to find the truth. But once you find it and recognize you are committed to it, you will move mountains and change yourself and the world: nothing can change you when you have this deeper sense of self and truth.

This is not egotistical; it is not that I am the best. It is recognizing that this is bigger than me, so I cannot give it up. That comes from deep humility and *bittul*. A parent moves mountains for a child, because the child is more important than himself. That is the idea of going to war: something more important than my life, for which I fight even if I must give my life.

That conviction comes from this deeper place, and it lets a person change the world. A person without it is just trying to be comfortable. You can bribe an employee, but he acts on a calculation of what gets him what he wants, and will not move mountains; he is stuck in his nature, and you can only stretch that so far. Changing one's nature and going beyond it requires this deeper perspective, the idea of *Israel*, *lamed rosh*.

A miracle for us is when we act that way; in *Elokus*, a miracle is when G-d reveals it. Someone asked the Rebbe whether you can do miracles, and he said that if everyone here, himself included, resolves to do something better, that will be our miracle. It is not a joke: resolving to change is our ability to go out of our nature and be masters of ourselves and the world.
blocks.title: A resolution as a miracle

blocks.text: This is the *shem mah* of *chachma*. And this is what the verse says, that you ruled over *Elokim*: we can rule over the *Elokim* of our nature and the nature of the world. *Dai lemevin*.
